title: August Visa Bulletin Warns EB-1 Green Cards for Indians Could Become Unavailable
excerpt: With EB-2 India already frozen for a third consecutive month, the State Department now signals that EB-1 India may also shut down before the fiscal year ends on September 30.
body:
• The State Department warns EB-1 India green cards could become unavailable in the coming weeks if demand exceeds the country's pro-rated allocation before September 30.
  • EB-2 India remains frozen at "unavailable" for a third straight month, with no new visas expected until FY 2027 opens on October 1.
  • EB-3 India is stuck at a January 1, 2014 cutoff date — meaning applicants who filed over 12 years ago are still waiting.
  • A separate USCIS policy shift pushing green card applicants toward consular processing abroad adds another layer of uncertainty for Indian professionals in the U.S.

The U.S. State Department's August 2026 Visa Bulletin delivers a sobering message for Indian nationals in the green card queue: the EB-1 category, long considered the fastest employment-based pathway for highly skilled workers, could be shut down within weeks.

The bulletin, released in late July, states that "high demand and number use by aliens chargeable to India in the EB-1 visa category may necessitate making the category unavailable in the coming weeks if India's pro-rated limit in the EB-1 category is reached before the fiscal year ends."

It is the first time this fiscal year the State Department has issued such a direct warning for EB-1 India, raising the prospect that all three major employment-based green card categories for Indian nationals could be frozen simultaneously before October 1.

EB-2 India: Three Months of Silence

The August bulletin confirms that EB-2 India remains marked "U" — unavailable — for the third consecutive month. The category hit its annual allocation limit earlier in 2026, and no new immigrant visa numbers can be issued until fiscal year 2027 begins on October 1.

EB-5 Unreserved for India is also unavailable, meaning Indian investors seeking permanent residency through the investor visa program face the same wall.

"EB-2 India reached its annual allocation limit earlier this year, and the Department of State cannot issue additional numbers in that category until FY 2027 begins on October 1, 2026."

— NPZ Law Group, August 2026 Visa Bulletin Analysis

Meanwhile, EB-3 India — the category covering skilled workers and professionals — holds at a final action date of January 1, 2014. That means applicants who filed their labor certifications more than 12 years ago are still awaiting their turn, a stark illustration of the backlog's depth.

What the Numbers Show

The August bulletin's Final Action Dates paint a clear picture of how unevenly the green card system treats applicants by country of birth:

For EB-1, India's cutoff sits at October 15, 2022, while applicants from most other countries face no backlog at all — their category is marked "current." China's EB-1 cutoff moved forward by one month to July 1, 2023.

For EB-2, India is unavailable while the rest of the world remains current. China's EB-2 holds at September 1, 2021.

For EB-3, India's January 2014 cutoff date is more than a decade behind the rest-of-world date of September 1, 2024.

USCIS has also mandated that employment-based applicants must use the Final Action Dates chart — not the more generous Dates for Filing chart — to determine eligibility for filing adjustment of status applications in August.

Consular Processing Shift Adds Pressure

Compounding the backlog frustration, a separate USCIS policy memorandum issued on May 22, 2026, has reframed adjustment of status — the process of applying for a green card from within the United States — as an "extraordinary form of relief" rather than the default option.

Under the directive, USCIS now treats consular processing at a U.S. embassy abroad as the standard pathway. Nonimmigrant visa holders, including those on H-1B and L-1 work visas, are expected to depart the country and complete their permanent residency applications from their home country except in "extraordinary circumstances."

"We are reverting to the law's original purpose to ensure that aliens properly navigate our nation's immigration system."

— Zach Kahler, USCIS Spokesman

For Indian professionals who have spent years — often over a decade — building careers and families in the United States while waiting for their priority dates to become current, being told to leave the country and process from abroad introduces risks of prolonged family separation, job loss, and re-entry complications.

What Comes Next

Immigration attorneys are advising clients in affected categories to stay in close contact with legal counsel as FY 2026 winds down. If EB-1 India does become unavailable, it would mark the first time in recent memory that EB-1, EB-2, and EB-5 for India are all simultaneously shut.

The earliest relief is expected when FY 2027 opens on October 1, 2026, when annual visa allocations reset. But the pace of any forward movement will depend on demand levels and whether Congress takes any action on the green card backlog, which currently exceeds one million applicants for Indian nationals alone.

For now, the message from the State Department is unambiguous: the window is narrowing, and time is running out before the fiscal year closes.
nri_angle: Indian professionals on H-1B and L-1 visas in the U.S. face deepening green card uncertainty as multiple employment-based categories stall or risk shutting down before the fiscal year ends.
author: Diaspora Desk
